full_judgment:
20. As to the question whether the owner was in Bangladesh after 25th March, 1971, will be considered later on. Now let us consider the legal matrix of the issue. Sub-section (2) of section 5 states that the lists published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence on the facts that the publication of the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have been vested in the government as such. There is no dispute that the disputed property has been enlisted in the `Kha' list. Therefore, there is presumption that the buildings have been vested in the government as abandoned property until and unless rebuttal evidence is produced by the claimants. Till the claimants can prove that they have right or interest in the property, there is conclusiveness of abandoned nature of the property. It is presumption of law. A presumption of law is a rule of law that a particular inference shall be drawn by a court of law from a particular circumstance. The rebuttable presumptions are intendments made by law, but unlike them, they only hold good until disproved. 

 21. In Bangladesh vs Jalil, 48 DLR (AD) 10, it has been held that section 5(2) of the Ordinance clearly provides that the lists published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have been vested in the government as such and that the government has no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property merely because the same is disputed by the claimant. In Government of Bangladesh vs Ashraf Ali, 49 DLR (AD) 161, it has been held that the listing of an abandoned property either in 'Ka' or `Kha' list is not a mistake or a default of the kind that makes the lists so prepared illegal. Once a particular property has been listed either in the 'Ka' list or `Kha' list there is natural presumption that it has been duly listed. Similar views have been taken in Bangladesh vs KM Zaker, 8 BLC (AD) 27. In Hazerullah vs Chairman, 1st Court of Settlement, 3 BLC (AD) 42, it has been observed that the government is under no obligation to prove anything after the enlistment of the property and the onus is on the claimant to prove otherwise. In CQMH Md. Ayub Ali vs Bangladesh, 47 DLR (AD) 71, it has been held that a building is included in the list is proof of its being an abandoned property, and the government has nothing to prove or deny. There are catenas of decisions of this Court on this point and at this stage it is not necessary to dwell with the said point. 

 26. It was held that she did not make any statement that her alleged husband subsequently gifted the disputed property by a deed; that Hosne Ara Begum never lived with Rafi Tehrani, which is also evident from the averments in the written deed of dated 18th October, 1972-she showed her place of residence at 277/2 Azimpur Road, Lalbagh, Dhaka; that the kabin nama is a forged one in that the signature of Rafi Tehrani in it does not tally with the admitted signature of Rafi Tehrani; that Rafi Tehrani never gifted the property in favour of Hosne Ara; that the other petitioner i.e. Abdus Sobhan did not admit that Raft Tehrani possessed this property or the alienation of the property in favour of Hosne Ara; that the address of Rail Tehrani in his deposition mentioned at Gulshan and in the kabin-nama he showed his address at Ispahani Colony which is corroborated by Abdus Sobhan; that Hosne Ara stated that Raft Tehrani left for London in the last part of 1975, whereas Hasina Tehrani's deposition shows that he was in Bara Magbazar till 1975; that Hosne Ara did not produce any tax receipts which proved that the City Corporation never recognized neither Zafar Tehrani nor Rafi Tehrani nor Hosne Ara as occupant of the property; that in the petition there is no averment that Zafar Tehrani made an oral gift in favour of Rafi Tehrani; that in the kabin-nama Hosne Ara's address was shown at 277/2 at Azimpur, Lalbagh and she was residing at that address which is evident from her admission in cross-examination that during the liberation period she lived with her father; that admittedly Hosne Ara sold the property to other applicants and after such transfer she has no subsisting right, title and interest in the case property; that the transfer is hit by PO 16 of 1972, inasmuch as, she sold the abandoned property which has been vested in the government; that Abdus Sobhan admitted that Advocate Abdur Rashid went into possession in the case property immediately after the liberation of Bangladesh which proved that he was not in possession on the day of promulgation of PO 16 of 1972 ; that the property has been rightly vested in the government; that non service of notice required under section 4(1)(b) was not challenged in the petition and that the appellants have failed to rebut the presumption of genuineness of listing of the property. These are findings of fact and these findings cannot be interfered with by the High Court Division hearing a writ of certiorari under article I 02(2)(ii) of the constitution. 

 69. From the impugned judgment and order, it further appears that respondent No.2, the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Public Works, filed affidavit-in-opposition in Writ Petition Nos.968 of 1995, 975 of 1995 and 1398 of 1995. In Writ Petition No.975 of 1995, respondent No.2 categorically stated that as the original owner, Rafi Tehrani, had left the country before P.0.16 of 1972 came into being, the same automatically vested in the Government by operation of law. Neither the Government nor the other rival claimants in the property in question, namely, Abdus Sobhan, the appellant in CA No. 77 of 2003, did challenge that Rafi Tehrani was not the son of Zafar Tehrani. It is apparent from the decision of the Court of Settlement that the appellants in Civil Appeal No.10 of 2003 in support of their case that Zafar Tehrani (father of Rafi Tehrani) purchased 0.18 acre land and 0.22 acre land respectively of CS Plot Nos.327 and 328 from Khan Mohammad Nuruddahar of village-Ratoil, PS Kakhiani, formerly Faridpur, now Gopalganj by registered deeds being Nos. 5173 and 5241 dated 23-6-1953; that Zafar Tehrani purchased the land of CS Plot No. 329 from Motilal Dey MajuMd.er in the benami of his wife, Amena Sultana, by registered deed No. 5331 dated 14-10-1947 ad the land of CS Plot Nos. 325, 326 and 322 from Fazle Ahmed Karim, Khan Bandur Md. Solaiman, Sagiruddin Ahmed Sorwardi and Fatema Fazle in the benami of Amena Sultana, Nargis Khanam and Rokeya Sultana, his wife and daughters respectively by registered kabalas being deed Nos. 3485 dated 23-2-1960 and 3484 dated 23-2-1960 and 4208 dated 9-3-1960 respectively filed the documents before it. The Court of Settlement kept those documents outside their consideration on the ground that those "were not put and proved into evidence and marked exts", though it considered the other documents filed by the appellants, which were also not formally proved into evidence. Thus the Court of Settlement followed two different standards to consider the documents filed before it by the appellants. It is very significant to note that all these transferred deeds were executed and registered at a time when nobody thought of a law in the form of PO 16 of 1972 or the Ordinance and under section 114(e) of the Evidence Act, these deeds have a presumption of correctness. Moreso, none challenged those deeds. It is also very pertinent to state that it was the specific case of the appellants that SA Khatians in respect of those plots were prepared in the name of Zafar Tehrani and the other purchasers and those were filed before the Court of Settlement as have been clearly mentioned in its decision. 

 123. The other reason assigned by the Court of Settlement in discarding the objection as to the non-service of notice under section 5( I)(b) of the Ordinance is that section 5(2) of the Ordinance attaches a presumption of correctness of the list prepared under section 5(1) of the Ordinance completely ignoring the fact that the Government failed to produce any scrap of paper to show that it took over possession thereof and/or that notice for surrendering or taking over possession was ever served upon the occupants, namely, the appellants. In taking the said view, the Court of Settlement failed to consider that the property in question was outside the scope of mischief of section 5 of the Ordinance, in view of the fact that the Ordinance itself prohibits the taking over possession unless a statutory notice is issued before the 31st October, 1988. In the context, it may be stated that as discussed above, in PO 16 of 1972, procedure to take over possession of an abandoned property has been laid down. And according to article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 if a person in possession of an abandoned property failed to surrender possession thereof as he is required to do under clause (2) thereof, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Officer or the authorized officer shall serve a notice on him in the prescribed manner requiring him to surrender possession of the property within seven days of the service of notice to the person mentioned in the notice or show cause against such surrender within the said period and if he fails to do so, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate or the authorized officer shall take possession of the property in such manner as may be prescribed of taking over possession of an abandoned property and, in fact, such procedure has been detailed in rule 3 of the Rules, 1972. And rule 3(8) of the Rules, 1972 has mandated that notice has to be served on the person in possession or on any adult male member of his family or, where none of them is available or they refuse to receive the notice, by affixing a copy of the notice to a conspicuous part of the residence of such person and also, where the abandoned property consists of any immovable property on a conspicuous part of such immovable property in the presence of two witnesses. And admittedly, in the instant case, no notice under article 7 of PO 16 of 1972 read with rule 3 of the Rules, 1972 was served. The provisions for service of notice upon the occupant of an abandoned property as provided in article 7 of PO 16 of 1972 read with rule 3 of the Rules, 1972 has, in fact, been re-introduced and re-asserted in clause (b) of section 5(1) of the Ordinance as a precondition before enlistment of a building of which the Government is not in possession and that notice for surrendering or taking over possession as abandoned property under PO 16 of 1972 had been served. 

 124. The Court of Settlement also failed to consider that the presumption attached to section 5 of the Ordinance is not sacrosanct and is rebuttable and in considering the presumption attached to section 5 of the Ordinance, it totally failed to consider the materials placed before it, particularly, the decree passed in Title Suit No.31 of 1972, the deposition of Rafi Tehrani in this suit, the order of the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar (South), Dhaka dropping the property of Purana Paltan of Rafi Tehrani from the list of abandoned buildings, the decree passed in Title Suit No.425 of 1978 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, First Court, Dhaka, the mutation khatian in the name of Hosne Ara Begum and the rent paid by her which prima facie proved that during the relevant period, i.e. 26-3-1971 to 28.021972, Rafi Tehrani was in possession of the property in question and subsequently he divested his ownership on Hosne Ara Begum, his wife, by oral gift and that she was in possession thereof. Therefore, the property in question did not answer the description of an abandoned property within the meaning of article 2(1) of PO 16 of 1972 and the presumption attached to section 5 of the Ordinance was very well rebutted. In the context, it is necessary to state that section 5 of the Ordinance does not say that to get a notice for surrendering or taking over possession as an abandoned property, one need be in possession of the entire property.
